content.summary: Welcome to your reading mission. In this lesson, you will read short texts about everyday digital habits and simple online safety rules. You will learn how to protect your personal information, manage your screen time, and understand important security advice using modal verbs and present simple sentences.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Modal verbs (should, shouldn't, must, need to) for advice and necessity, and Present Simple for daily routines.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Digital habits, passwords, screen time, privacy settings, and cybersecurity terms.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming the text for general meaning and scanning for specific security tips or details.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short A2 texts about digital habits.
Locate specific details such as password rules and screen time limits.
Recognize and practice grammar patterns with modal verbs and imperatives.

contextWarmup.prompt: What is the best way to keep your social media account safe from strangers?
options: Use your birthday as your password
Keep your privacy settings private and use a strong password
Share your login details with your best friend
contextWarmup.explanation: Keeping your privacy settings private and using a strong password protects your personal data from unknown users.

rules: Use should and shouldn't to give friendly advice about online safety, such as you should change your password regularly.
Use must, mustn't, and need to to express strong rules and necessity, such as you must verify links before clicking.
Use imperative sentences for direct instructions and warnings, such as never share your password with anyone.

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often mix up should and must. Should is for general advice, while must is for strict rules and strong necessity.
commonTrap.wrong: You must wear a blue shirt when you log in online.
commonTrap.correct: You should use a strong password to protect your accounts.

grammarFormulas.title: Sentence Patterns with Modal Verbs
grammarFormulas.description: Assemble sentence blocks to practice rules and advice:

items.exampleSentence: You should create a strong password with letters and numbers.
I try to limit my screen time to two hours a day.
You need to check your privacy settings on social media regularly.
Always verify links before clicking on them.
Be careful of online scams that ask for your personal information.
Don't open attachments from unknown senders.
If an email looks suspicious, delete it immediately.
You should enable two-factor authentication for better security.
Remember to update your apps and software regularly.
Only download files from trusted websites.

content.passageTitle: Smart Digital Habits for Everyday Life
paragraphs: Today, teenagers spend a lot of screen time on phones, tablets, and computers. We check social media every morning, chat with friends, and download fun apps. However, being online every day means we need to follow basic cybersecurity rules. Protecting your personal information is very important.

First, you should create a strong password with letters, numbers, and symbols. Never share your password with anyone, even your friends. Second, check your privacy settings on social media regularly so strangers cannot see your photos. If you receive an email with a strange link or an unknown file to attach, be careful because it might be a scam.

Finally, always verify links before clicking on them. If an email looks suspicious, delete it immediately. You should also enable two-factor authentication for extra security and remember to update your apps and software regularly to keep your devices safe from online threats.

content.summary: Develop essential listening skills for understanding conversations about digital habits and cybersecurity. Practice catching key details about online threats, passwords, and screen time while noticing how words connect in spoken English.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken conversation about online safety.
Identify details such as passwords, scams, and screen time.
Notice how words link together in connected speech.

keyPhrases.note: Used to describe fraudulent emails trying to steal personal information.
Controls who can view your profile and photos on social media.
A secure combination of letters, numbers, and special symbols.
The total amount of time spent looking at a phone or computer screen.

connectedSpeech.note: The sound /d/ and /j/ merge into /dʒ/ in fast natural speech.
Final consonant /t/ links smoothly into the starting consonant /f/.
The final /d/ in need links directly to the weak vowel in a.
The preposition of often reduces to schwa /əv/ in fast conversation.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Modern Digital Habits & Online Cybersecurity Basics

content.summary: Practical guide on sentence structure and paragraph building in English for discussing digital habits, screen time, and basic cybersecurity rules using modal verbs and imperatives.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Giving Advice with Should and Shouldn't
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + should / shouldn't + base verb + complement
blueprintItems.example: You should use a strong password for your email accounts.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Expressing Rules with Must and Mustn't
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + must / mustn't + base verb + complement
blueprintItems.example: You must keep your private information safe online.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Writing Direct Instructions with Imperatives
blueprintItems.example: Never click on unknown links in suspicious messages.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize platform names, applications, and proper nouns correctly.
mechanicsRules.badExample: we check our instagram accounts every morning.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: We check our Instagram accounts every morning.
mechanicsRules.why: Names of specific platforms like Instagram are proper nouns and require capitalization.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use apostrophes correctly in negative modal and auxiliary contractions.
mechanicsRules.badExample: You shouldnt share your personal details online.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: You shouldn't share your personal details online.
mechanicsRules.why: Contractions like shouldn't and mustn't require an apostrophe between the n and the t.

mechanicsRules.rule: End imperative sentences and safety rules with a clear full stop or exclamation mark.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Always check the sender email address
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Always check the sender email address.
mechanicsRules.why: Every complete sentence in English must end with appropriate punctuation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the following affirmative sentence into a complete negative sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: I check my social media accounts every hour.
targetAnswers: I don't check my social media accounts every hour.
I do not check my social media accounts every hour.
practicumQuestions.explanation: With the first-person subject 'I', use 'don't' or 'do not' followed by the base verb 'check'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the modal verb 'should' for advice:
practicumQuestions.promptText: It is a good idea to update your software.
practicumQuestions.explanation: To give advice at A2 level, replace 'It is a good idea to' with 'You should' followed by the base verb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the two sentences using the conjunction 'because':
practicumQuestions.promptText: I changed my password. It was weak.
targetAnswers: I changed my password because it was weak.
I changed my password because it was too weak.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The conjunction 'because' connects an action with its reason.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalization and punctuation in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: we must verify links before clicking them on twitter.
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize the first word and the proper noun Twitter.
targetAnswers: We must verify links before clicking them on Twitter.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Sentences must start with a capital letter, and platform names like Twitter require capitalization.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fill in the blank with the correct negative modal verb for a strict rule:
practicumQuestions.promptText: You _____ share your personal passwords with strangers.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'mustn't' or 'must not' to express prohibition or strict rules.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change this statement into a direct imperative instruction:
practicumQuestions.promptText: You need to be careful when downloading files.
practicumQuestions.hint: Start directly with the base verb 'Be'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Imperative sentences omit the subject pronoun and start directly with the base verb.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the clauses using the conjunction 'but':
practicumQuestions.promptText: I want to check my email. My internet connection is down.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'but' to connect the contrasting ideas.
targetAnswers: I want to check my email, but my internet connection is down.
I want to check my email but my internet connection is down.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'but' to link two clauses that show contrast or opposition.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the missing apostrophe error in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: You shouldnt click on suspicious email links.
targetAnswers: You shouldn't click on suspicious email links.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Contractions such as shouldn't require an apostrophe between n and t.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the digital security collocation in the sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Always use a strong _________ for your email account.
practicumQuestions.hint: The missing word refers to a secret combination of letters and numbers.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The standard security collocation is 'strong password'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change this rule into a negative imperative sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: It is important that you do not open strange attachments.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Negative imperatives start with 'Never' or 'Do not' followed by the base verb.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Modern Digital Habits & Online Cybersecurity Basics

content.summary: This guide helps you speak clearly about daily digital habits, screen time, and online safety at an A2 level.
content.audioGuidance: Focus on clear consonant clusters in words like screen and strong, and pronounce vowel sounds accurately in technical words like password and update.

pillars.name: Vowel Clarity
pillars.target: Clear short and long vowels in digital terms
pillars.explanation: Pronounce vowels distinctly in words like password, screen, and update so listeners understand you easily.

pillars.name: Consonant Clusters
pillars.explanation: Practice consonant blends at the start of words, such as scr in screen and str in strong, without adding extra vowel sounds.

pillars.name: Sentence Stress
pillars.explanation: Put more volume and pitch on important words like verbs and nouns, while keeping grammar words softer.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice how the stress shifts and adapts when the noun expands into a compound modifier.
The stress moves to the second syllable in the past participle form.
Stress shifts from the first syllable to the second syllable when changing from noun to adjective.
Longer noun derivations move the primary stress closer to the suffix.
